Mehta also found that the doctrine of consular non-reviewability, which generally shields those decisions from judicial review, does not block consideration of the case because it challenged a State Department policy.His order enjoined the State Department from applying the public charge policy to De Moura Gomes’ visa request and from adjudicating his application when it’s deemed complete by a consular officer.The State Department policy is blatantly unlawful and fundamentally unfair, said Edward Ramos, a partner at Kurzban Kurzban Tetzeli and Pratt P.A. and counsel for De Moura Gomes.“We are pleased the Court recognized that the State Department cannot require individualized review and then dictate refusal regardless of the result,” he said in a statement. “Congress entrusted visa decisions to consular officers applying the law to each case. This policy stripped them of that judgment and predetermined the outcome.”A State Department spokesperson told Bloomberg that the agency doesn’t comment on ongoing litigation as a general matter, but added that the Trump administration is “upholding the highest standards of screening and vetting of visa applicants.”
Article Summary: Judge Amit Mehta of the US District Court for the District of Columbia ruled that the State Department's Green Card ban for 75 countries is illegal. The public charge policy issued by Secretary of State Marco Rubio is an exercise of authority specifically denied by Congress in the Immigration and Nationality Act, he said.

Article Title: US researchers tracked nearly 450 coastal wetlands for up to 20 years; 84% were sinking towards open water and only 16% kept pace with rising seas
Article Text:
Representative image

How the study worked

What the researchers found

Why the Gulf Coast is hit hardest

Inland migration could save some wetlands

Why this matters for people too

A warning, but not a dead end

A new nationwide study suggests that most coastal wetlands in the contiguous United States are struggling to keep up with rising sea levels. Researchers tracking nearly 450 wetlands for up to 20 years found that 84% are gradually being inundated, putting many on a path to become open water if current trends continue. The study is published in Earth's Future. The finding is a big deal because coastal wetlands are not just patches of marshland. They help buffer storm surge, protect roads and buildings, and provide habitat for birds, fish and other wildlife. In other words, when wetlands disappear, the loss is ecological, economic and social all at once."Our study provides wetland managers with new information to help them make better-informed decisions and identify meaningful solutions to issues they may be encountering, including facilitating wetland migration upslope," Glenn Guntenspergen, U.S. Geological Survey's coastal wetland ecologist and senior author on the study, said, according to Phys.org.To get a national picture, researchers used elevation data from nearly 450 monitoring stations along the Atlantic, Gulf and Pacific coasts. They compared those measurements with tide-gauge data to see which wetlands were building elevation fast enough to stay above rising water and which ones were falling behind.That kind of long-term fieldwork is hard to do at scale. Wetland researchers have to work in muddy, remote terrain with specialised equipment, and some sites are only accessible by boat or even helicopter. The result is that national-level data on wetland change have been limited until now.The headline result is sobering: 89% of wetlands are gaining some elevation through sediment buildup, but only 16% are doing so fast enough to outpace sea-level rise. The rest are slowly sinking into a future where tides overtake them more often and, eventually, permanently.That does not mean every wetland is doomed, though. The study found important regional differences, with the Atlantic Coast generally holding up better than the Gulf Coast. Some wetlands may still have a chance to survive if they can build sediment quickly enough or migrate inland into available space.The Gulf Coast appears to be the most vulnerable region in the study. Researchers pointed to a mix of sea-level rise and human pressures, including altered river flow, reduced sediment supply and land subsidence linked to oil and gas extraction. Those factors make it harder for wetlands to stay elevated and healthy.By contrast, some Atlantic Coast wetlands are faring better because they receive more marine sediment from ocean waves, which helps them keep pace with the water. But even there, the study suggests that resilience is not guaranteed.One of the most important takeaways from the research is that wetlands are not all trapped in place. The study found that 73% of the wetlands still have some opportunity to move inland, as long as the land behind them is low enough and not blocked by roads, levees, buildings or other development.That matters because wetland survival is often about space as much as water. If land managers protect inland “migration corridors,” restore natural sediment flow or remove barriers such as dikes, some wetlands may be able to relocate instead of drowning where they stand.Wetlands deliver enormous benefits to human communities. They absorb storm energy, reducing damage from surges and flooding, and they support hunting, birdwatching and tourism. The study’s authors note that these ecosystems provide trillions of dollars in services each year across the United States.That makes wetland loss more than an environmental issue. It becomes a planning issue, a public safety issue and a climate adaptation issue. The more wetlands disappear, the more vulnerable coastal communities may become to storms and flooding.The researchers say the study should help managers make more informed decisions, especially about where to focus conservation efforts. In practical terms, that may mean protecting inland spaces, restoring sediment flows, or even using managed retreat in some areas to give wetlands room to move.The message is serious, but not hopeless. As one of the study’s authors put it, the paper shows not only where wetlands are in trouble, but also where conservation efforts could have the biggest effect.
Article Summary: Researchers tracked nearly 450 wetlands for up to 20 years. 84% are gradually being inundated, putting many on a path to become open water if current trends continue. Gulf Coast appears to be the most vulnerable region in the study. Some wetlands may still have a chance to survive if they can build sediment quickly enough or migrate inland into available space.

Article Title: Meet Darshan Magdum, Indian member of US boy band, who finally gets O-1 visa and the Internet is behind it
Article Text:
Darshan Magdum announces to his band members in the US that he got his O-1 visa.

What is Boy Throb?

Darshan Magdum, an Indian vocalist, called his band members in the US on FaceTime to announce that his visa has been approved. "We did it, guys," Magdum told his bandmates Zachary Sobania, Evan Papier and Anthony Key. Four of them are believed to be Boy Throb, a viral boy band about which not much is known. Their virality was born on the Internet and the visa battle too. There were many Reddit theories on whether Boy Throb is a real band or whether Darshan Magdum was a real person or not.Darshan's visa battle started in December 2025. He wanted to come to the US for a tour with this new band which was till then only confined to the Internet. Immigration officials returned his appeal with a request for evidence, the Washington Post reported. The band had to prove that they were a real band so that Darshan could be granted a visa.The band then started its tour without Darshan and the demands for Darshan's visa rose even from the audience when Darshan appeared via Zoom in those concert.According to The Guardian, Boy Throb formed last fall, and the name was chosen from social media only. Evan Papier, Anthony Key, and Zachary Sobania, the three other members, live in Los Angeles.Dressed in pink, they started singing covers of familiar pop hits but then replaced the lyrics to persuade the government to approve Magdum's visa. Their goal was to reach a million followers to support his application.O-1 visa is designated for people with extraordinary abilities, and now Internet personalities too apply for this visa.In March, Boy Throb shared with fans that the government had requested more information to support Magdum’s application. “Begging for press solely to improve an immigration beneficiary request is not indicative of an organization or an establishment that has a distinguished reputation,” the letter said.Boy Throb connected with Jonathan Grode, an immigration lawyer based in Pennsylvania, who submitted additional paperwork to support Magdum’s visa application. “This case really caught my attention because they knew that they had people with talent, they knew they had people with an idea, but they let the fame come before the recognition of the ability,” Grode said to The Guardian. “It fundamentally begs the question of: how is fame created?”

He wanted to come to the US for a tour with this new band which was till then only confined to the Internet.

Article Title: The US army built a 1,500-mile Alaska Highway through wilderness in just eight months during World War II
Article Text:
What is Alaska Highway and its importance in history

Why the Alaska Highway was necessary

Building a highway at breakneck speed

The crews worked 24 hours a day, through dense forests, frozen ground, rivers and mountainous terrain to make the highway

The trials of building through the wilderness

A road that changed the North

As per ASCE, following construction, the U.S. Public Roads Administration converted the road for civilian use

What is the condition of the Alaska Highway currently

Imagine building a 1,500-mile road across frozen forests, high mountains, swamps and permafrost in less than a year. It sounds like an impossible engineering task, but that is exactly what the U.S. Army did during World War II. According to the American Society of Civil Engineers website, one of the most ambitious military construction projects in North American history was the Alaska Highway, built under pressure after Pearl Harbor was attacked. It was more than a road, it was a symbol of international cooperation, wartime urgency and human endurance under some of the toughest natural conditions on earth.Alaska, although part of the United States, lies geographically apart from the other 48 states, separated by Canada. According to reports, in the 1920s, the U.S. proposed a highway through Canada to link Alaska with the mainland. But Canada was reluctant, since the project was expensive and the areas it would link—the Yukon, British Columbia and Alaska—were sparsely populated. That all changed when Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941.The highway suddenly became a military necessity, with the threat of more strikes along the western coast of North America. It would provide a safe land route for transporting troops, equipment and supplies to Alaska, which had become strategically important during the war.The ASCE website states that Canada agreed to the United States’ building of the highway on the condition that when the war was over, the Canadian portion of the road was to revert to Canadian control. And then, construction officially started in March 1942 for which more than 10,000 American troops, many of them from Army engineering units, and civilian workers were sent in. Trains carried north vast amounts of heavy machinery, construction equipment and supplies.And the crews worked 24 hours a day, through dense forests, frozen ground, rivers and mountainous terrain. Late in September 1942, the parties moving from opposite directions met at mile 588. The highway was declared substantially complete in late October and a formal dedication ceremony was held at Soldier's Summit on November 20, 1942. Interestingly, the whole 1,500 mile route was completed in only eight months.While the road was technically finished, it was far from perfect. Much of it was rough gravel surface with tight switchbacks, temporary pontoon bridges and very few guardrails. Many stretches were built with "corduroy roads," logs laid across soft ground to prevent the surface from sinking, states online data. It is also reported that in the spring thaw of 1943, melting permafrost caused hundreds of miles of the highway to fall apart. Later, engineers spent months fixing damaged sections before the road could be reliably used later that year. Construction crews also faced brutal winters with temperatures as low as minus 40 degrees. Workers were often forced to build fires under frozen machinery and pour oil on the flames just to keep the engines running, according to the 1944 Canadian government documentary Pincers on Japan.Ironically, the Alaska Highway did not play as much of a military role as had been anticipated. Most of the wartime movement of troops and supplies continued by sea, while the U.S. Army Transport Service used hundreds of barges, tugboats, fishing vessels and other small craft to support operations in Alaska. Still, the highway changed northern transportation for ever. As per ASCE, following construction, the U.S. Public Roads Administration converted the road for civilian use. The Canadian portion was returned to Canada in 1946, and the highway was officially opened to the public in 1948.Today’s Alaska Highway bears little resemblance to its wartime origins. Today it is one of the most scenic road trips in North America with modern pavement, permanent steel and concrete bridges, better drainage, and regular maintenance. The highway stretches from Dawson Creek, British Columbia to Delta Junction, Alaska and draws thousands of tourists, adventurers and road trip enthusiasts every year.Images Courtesy: istock
Article Summary: The Alaska Highway was built by the U.S. Army during World War II. The 1,500-mile route was completed in only eight months. It was a symbol of international cooperation, wartime urgency and human endurance. Today it is one of the most scenic road trips in North America.

Article Title: When Jeff Bezos asked his team to help after a rainforest charity saving the Amazon said it was blocked from using 'Amazon' in Google Ads
Article Text:
Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Jeff Bezos' response to the Amazon Google Ads dispute

Was Amazon preventing the charity from using the word?

What is Junglekeepers?

Why the Amazon rainforest is so important

Did Jeff Bezos donate to Junglekeepers?

A campaign to protect one of the world's most important rainforests took an unexpected turn when conservationist Paul Rosolie revealed that his organisation, Junglekeepers, had difficulty using the word "Amazon" in Google Ads while promoting its work. Frustrated by what he described as an automated trademark-related obstacle, Rosolie turned to Amazon founder Jeff Bezos through Instagram, asking for help. Bezos responded publicly, saying he would have his team look into the matter. Rosolie later confirmed that the issue had been resolved, bringing attention not only to the unusual advertising hurdle but also to Junglekeepers' mission to protect large areas of Peru's Amazon rainforest from illegal logging, mining and poaching, while highlighting the challenges environmental organisations can face when using digital platforms to raise awareness and attract public support.In early May 2026, wildlife conservationist Paul Rosolie, founder of Junglekeepers, revealed on Instagram that his organisation was struggling to promote its rainforest conservation campaigns because Google Ads had flagged its use of the word "Amazon." According to Rosolie, the apparent trademark-related restriction made it difficult for the charity to advertise its work to protect the Amazon rainforest.Hoping to resolve the issue, he publicly tagged Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos in a post explaining the situation.Bezos responded from his verified Instagram account shortly afterwards, writing, "This makes no sense. Having the team reach out to help." Rosolie later confirmed that Bezos' team contacted Junglekeepers and helped resolve the Google Ads issue, allowing the charity to continue promoting its conservation efforts. While there is no evidence that Bezos personally changed Google's advertising policies or Amazon's trademark rules, his intervention helped bring a swift resolution to the problem and drew wider attention to Junglekeepers' mission in Peru's Amazon rainforest.Despite the headlines surrounding the incident, there is no evidence that Amazon.com intentionally stopped Junglekeepers from using the word "Amazon." The problem appears to have stemmed from Google's automated trademark review process for advertisements rather than any direct legal action by Amazon.Like many global companies, Amazon owns numerous registered trademarks covering its products and services. However, trademark protection applies only to specific commercial categories and does not grant exclusive ownership of the geographical name "Amazon." The rainforest, river and surrounding region continue to be widely referred to by their historic name, and the reported issue appears to have been an advertising platform error rather than a trademark dispute.Junglekeepers is a non-profit conservation organisation founded by wildlife conservationist and author Paul Rosolie. The organisation works to protect sections of the Peruvian Amazon by purchasing or securing vulnerable rainforest land and employing local and Indigenous forest rangers to safeguard it.Its work focuses on preventing illegal logging, gold mining, poaching and land grabbing while maintaining forest trails, monitoring wildlife and preserving biodiversity. According to the organisation, it has already protected around 138,000 acres of rainforest and is working to secure another 170,000 acres through ongoing fundraising efforts.The Amazon rainforest is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth, spanning nine South American countries and supporting an extraordinary range of wildlife and plant species. Scientists consider it one of the planet's most important ecosystems because it stores vast amounts of carbon, influences rainfall patterns and plays a critical role in regulating the global climate.Junglekeepers operates in Peru's Madre de Dios region and the Las Piedras watershed, an area recognised as one of the world's richest biodiversity hotspots. However, the region also faces growing threats from illegal mining, logging, road construction and wildlife trafficking, making conservation efforts increasingly urgent.Although Jeff Bezos stepped in to help resolve the Google Ads issue, there is no public evidence that he personally donated to Junglekeepers following the incident.Bezos has, however, made significant commitments to environmental causes through the Bezos Earth Fund, which he launched in 2020 with a pledge of $10 billion for climate and nature initiatives through 2030. The fund supports projects related to forest conservation, biodiversity, climate science and ecosystem restoration around the world.The episode highlighted an unusual irony: a charity working to save the Amazon rainforest found itself struggling to advertise using the word "Amazon." While the issue appears to have been caused by automated advertising systems rather than deliberate action by Amazon, it demonstrated how digital platforms can sometimes create unexpected barriers for conservation organisations.
Article Summary: conservationist Paul Rosolie revealed his organisation, Junglekeepers, had difficulty using the word "Amazon" in Google Ads while promoting its work. He publicly tagged Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos in a post explaining the situation. Bezos responded publicly, saying he would have his team look into the matter. There is no evidence that Bezos personally changed Google's advertising policies or Amazon's trademark rules.

Article Title: 'Long history of unlawful violence': Global watchdogs condemn Pakistan's crackdown in PoK
Article Text:
PoK (File photo)

As Pakistan-occupied Kashmir goes through its so-called assembly polls, reports of brutality, violence and unrest continue to surface, with global human rights and press freedom watchdogs raising alarm over an escalating crackdown on protesters and the media.International organisations, including Amnesty International and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), have flagged allegations of state-backed violence, restrictions on independent reporting, enforced disappearances of journalists and prolonged internet shutdowns. They have urged Pakistani authorities to end the crackdown, restore communication services and ensure transparent investigations into alleged human rights violations.Highlighting reports of excessive force used against demonstrators in Rawalakot, Amnesty International said the incidents reflected Pakistan's long record of using unlawful violence against protesters."The disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot are consistent with the Pakistani authorities' long history of unlawful violence against protesters. A prompt, independent, and transparent investigation must be ordered into the security forces' use of force against protesters.So long as an internet and mobile services blackout remains in place, it will severely impede the independent verification of the full extent of the situation on the ground. We urge the Pakistani authorities to restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area," Amnesty said in a post on X.Echoing similar concerns, CPJ said it was monitoring the deteriorating press freedom situation in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, citing internet blackouts, telecommunications shutdowns, reporting restrictions and the detention and disappearance of journalists.The press freedom watchdog also expressed concern over the reported disappearance of independent journalist Razi Tahir and his colleague Muhammad Saif, who were allegedly taken by men in police uniforms from their office in Islamabad on August 1."CPJ is deeply concerned by reports that independent journalist Razi Tahir and his colleague Muhammad Saif have been missing since August 1. They were reportedly taken by men in police uniforms from their office in Islamabad, and their whereabouts remain unknown. Pakistani authorities must acknowledge whether they are in state custody, ensure due process, and immediately release them if they are being arbitrarily detained," it wrote.In a subsequent update, CPJ said the two journalists remain missing while Kashmiri journalist Raja Ikram, who was reportedly detained in Islamabad on August 1, has since been released."Journalists Razi Tahir and Muhmmad Saif remain missing after reportedly being taken by men in police uniform on August 1. Pakistani authorities must acknowledge their detention if they are in state custody, ensure due process, and immediately release them. Kashmiri journalist Raja Ikram, who was reportedly detained in Islamabad on August 1, was later released," it added.CPJ also said the media crackdown appears to be extending beyond the region, pointing to reported action against major news outlets alongside continuing telecommunications disruptions.The criticism comes as casualties continue to mount during the ongoing protest movement. According to figures released by the Human Rights Council of Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir (HRC-PoJK) as of Sunday, at least 80 people have died, including 33 civilians before July 27, 43 people killed since July 27 across Rawalakot, Mirpur and Muzaffarabad, and four Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir police personnel.
Article Summary: Watchdogs raise alarm over escalating crackdown on protesters and the media. Amnesty International, Committee to Protect Journalists have flagged allegations of state-backed violence, restrictions on independent reporting and enforced disappearances of journalists. They have urged Pakistani authorities to end the crackdown, restore communication services and ensure transparent investigations.
