Article Title: 'They'll arrest us at hospitals': PoK protesters risk death over electricity, flour demands
Article Text:
Dozens killed in PoK as protesters treating gunshot wounds in makeshift clinics avoid hospitals for fear of arrest

Makeshift clinic treats dozens of critically injured

JAAC and authorities trade accusations

Food shortages, roadblocks add to tensions

A protest movement in PoK has escalated into deadly clashes between security forces and demonstrators, with dozens of people reportedly killed across the region in recent weeks, the BBC reported.The protests have been led by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), which has been demanding cheaper electricity and flour as well as better access to education, healthcare and other basic services. The movement says an agreement reached with the governments of Pakistan and PoK in October to address some of its demands has not been implemented.The BBC reported that Rawalakot, one of the main centres of the protests, was experiencing severe disruption, with roads blocked, shops shut and internet access cut off.The BBC visited a makeshift clinic near the main protest site, where a spare bedroom had been converted into a medical supply area and a bed placed outside beneath a tarpaulin was being used to treat injured protesters.A doctor identified by the BBC as Dr Anwar said the clinic had treated around 50 to 60 critically injured people since July 27, including an estimated 15 to 20 people with gunshot wounds.The doctor said the facility could provide basic emergency treatment, including stopping bleeding, dressing wounds and removing superficial bullets, but lacked the equipment required for serious injuries involving the chest, abdomen, head or other vital organs.He also said protesters were reluctant to seek treatment at the main hospital because of fears they could be arrested or shot there. Authorities have rejected that claim.The BBC spoke to families who said relatives had been shot during the protests. One woman, identified as Asma, said she was at a demonstration when she learned that her only son had been shot. Another man, Salman, told the BBC that his younger brother had died.The JAAC says its demonstrations are peaceful and focused on economic and basic-rights demands. The group has rejected allegations that it is responsible for violence, while authorities have accused it of being armed and attempting to disrupt ongoing elections in the region.The JAAC was banned in June and labelled foreign-funded terrorists by the authorities, according to the BBC. The group rejected the characterisation and said its financial support was from the PoK diaspora and not India, an accusation that Pakistan has tried to make on multiple occasions.Authorities have also accused the group of attacking law-enforcement personnel and obstructing public order. Officials have released drone footage that they said showed JAAC members carrying guns on rooftops and displayed weapons they said had been recovered from the group.The government has rejected allegations that security forces fired indiscriminately at peaceful protesters, saying law-enforcement personnel acted against people involved in attacks on security forces, threats to public safety or obstruction of lawful authority.The JAAC, meanwhile, has alleged that security forces were responsible for firing on protesters. Umar Nazir, a member of the group's core committee, also alleged that people had infiltrated the movement and may have carried out violence to support the authorities' narrative, though he provided no evidence for the claim.The BBC said that during protests it attended, its journalists saw no weapons or shooting among demonstrators, although gunshots were heard overnight and it could not establish who was firing or at what.The unrest has also disrupted supplies in Rawalakot. The BBC reported seeing food shortages, with most shops closed and protesters sharing available food. Some residents described attempts to smuggle rice into the city.Several roads have been blocked by fallen trees and other debris. Authorities have blamed the JAAC for the blockades, while also denying that they were preventing food or medical supplies from reaching Rawalakot.The protests come as local elections are taking place in PoK, adding another layer of tension to the confrontation.
Article Summary: Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) has been demanding cheaper electricity and flour as well as better access to education, healthcare and other basic services. The BBC visited a makeshift clinic near the main protest site, where a spare bedroom had been converted into a medical supply area. A doctor said the clinic had treated around 50 to 60 critically injured people since July 27.

Article Title: '15-year-olds shot, only asked for basic rights': Inside the deadly PoK crackdown
Article Text:
Deadly clashes continue during protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir

'Most victims were 15 to 35'

'We are not terrorists'

Teenagers as young as 15 have been among those killed or seriously injured in a sweeping crackdown on protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), according to a report by the BBC based on the accounts of residents, doctors and families from the protest hub of Rawalakot. The demonstrations in Rawalakot by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) have turned deadly amid an ongoing security operation.The report said that dozens of people have been killed across the region over the past two months in clashes between security forces and protesters. The demonstrations comes as local elections are underway in the region.A doctor identified as Dr Anwar said that he had treated 50 to 60 critically injured patients since July 27, including 15 to 20 people with gunshot wounds."Most of those who have been killed or seriously injured are young people between about 15-16 years old and 32-35 years old. I have seen very few patients over the age of 40," BBC quoted the doctor saying.According to the report, many injured protesters have avoided government hospitals fearing arrest or being shot, a claim denied by the authorities.Families of those killed described the protests as a movement for basic rights, including affordable electricity, flour, education and healthcare."We only asked for affordable flour, electricity and our basic rights," Ali, whose friend Shafqat Hussain was fatally shot, told the BBC. "Instead, our brothers are being killed. What was our crime? Why are live bullets being fired at us?"Asma, whose only son was killed, said: "We were only asking for our rights. We are not terrorists." She added, "He knew there were risks, but he believed standing up for justice was important. He used to say that dying for a just cause was an honour."Another resident, Salman, whose younger brother died during the protests, told the BBC: "He was the youngest in the family and was loved by everyone... I feel proud that he gave his life while standing up for the rights of the people. He was not fighting or attacking anyone."The JAAC says the protests stem from the government's failure to implement an agreement signed in October that promised relief on electricity prices and other public welfare issues.The group, which was banned in June and designated by authorities as a foreign-funded terrorist organisation, denies the allegation, insisting it is a peaceful movement funded by the PoK diaspora.The Pakistan-occupied Kashmir government has rejected allegations that security forces fired indiscriminately at peaceful protesters. It said law enforcement acted only against individuals involved in attacks on security personnel, threats to public safety or obstruction of lawful authority.
Article Summary: Dozens of people have been killed across the region over the past two months in clashes between security forces and protesters. The demonstrations in Rawalakot by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) have turned deadly amid an ongoing security operation. The Pakistan-occupied Kashmir government has rejected allegations that security forces fired indiscriminately at peaceful protesters.

Article Title: 'Do not befriend Kaafirs': Pakistani general levels terror allegations against India
Article Text:
Pakistan's military spokesperson Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry

Pakistan's military spokesperson, Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, has sparked controversy after saying in a video that Muslims should not befriend "kaafirs" (non-believers), warning that those who do would no longer be considered among the faithful."Do not befriend kaafirs (non-believers) and leave the faithful. If you do that, there's a problem. Then you are not among the Muslims," Chaudhry said while addressing a press conference.“Now our population is 240-250 million people, and we still have four provinces. We have to see whether this is serving the purpose of good governance. That debate has to be sensibly held by politicians, by those in power, even those who have previously been in power, and those who are responsible to the people of Pakistan,” he added.The remarks were made during a wider media briefing that focused on Pakistan's counter-terrorism operations, the security situation in Balochistan, and the country's ties with Afghanistan.Taking a jibe at India-Afghanistan ties, Chaudhry claimed that the Afghan Taliban regime's "business" was terrorism, alleging that it used militancy to sustain its economy, state institutions and diplomacy.“Even their diplomacy is centred on terrorism. What is common between India and Afghanistan, except their DNA? The only thing common is terrorism,” Chaudhary said, as cited by Dawn.Chaudhry also claimed that around 300 Indian websites were being used to support terrorism-related activities in Balochistan, while more than 1,000 social media accounts and what he described as a "hostile diaspora" were involved in spreading propaganda linked to terrorism.“First, an event or incident is seeded, right or wrong, and then it is framed by initiators, who hand it over to amplifiers. Then mass amplification is done by mainstream Indian media, channels and their print media as well, from where it is picked up by international media, and then you take it and run it as facts," he said.The DG ISPR said the government was also working to strengthen the police force, including by deploying newly recruited assistant superintendents of police (ASPs) to Balochistan and providing bulletproof vehicles, among other measures.The remarks come amid a series of attacks on Pakistani security forces across Balochistan last month, with armed clashes also reported during military operations in the Mastung and Kech districts, according to The Balochistan Post (TBP).The insurgency in Balochistan has been led by several separatist groups, including the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), which has waged a long-running campaign against Pakistan's federal government. The group has frequently targeted security personnel and infrastructure in the province and has also carried out attacks in other parts of the country, including Karachi.According to Pakistan's 2023 census, Balochistan is home to around 15 million people and is rich in natural resources, including coal, gold, copper and natural gas. The BLA maintains that these resources should belong to the people of Balochistan and opposes the federal government's control over their extraction and the province's security.
Article Summary: Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Muslims should not befriend "kaafirs" (non-believers) He warned that those who do would no longer be considered among the faithful. The remarks were made during a wider media briefing on Pakistan's counter-terrorism operations.

Article Title: Pakistan restricts digital news websites reporting on PoK protests, crackdowns: Report
Article Text:
Pakistan expands online curbs following coverage of PoK unrest

Pakistan has reportedly expanded digital censorship measures by restricting access to several news websites following extensive media coverage of the ongoing unrest in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK).Alongside the reported blocking of local and regional news websites, international broadcasters, have also become inaccessible to users in parts of Pakistan, according to media reports cited by ANI.The restrictions appear to target platforms covering the recent protests, alleged security crackdowns and growing public discontent in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK). Pakistani authorities have not officially confirmed the reported restrictions.The channels facing possible blocking include those linked to Pakistan's main opposition party, its leader and jailed former prime minister Imran Khan, as well as several journalists critical of the government, according to a court order dated June 24.Earlier in July, Al Jazeera reported that a judicial magistrate's court in Islamabad had ordered the blocking of several YouTube channels based on a June 2 report by Pakistan's National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA).The agency alleged that the channels had published content that was "intimidating", "provocative" and "derogatory" towards state institutions and public officials.Al Jazeera reported that digital rights groups have warned the proposed bans could further restrict freedom of expression in Pakistan. With television and print media facing significant curbs, social media remains one of the few platforms for public debate and dissent, the report said.The broadcaster also reported that YouTube had notified 27 content creators that their channels could be blocked if they failed to comply with the court's directives.The restrictions come amid heightened sensitivity over the flow of information related to the political situation and local protests in PoK.The second phase of elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) was marred by widespread disruptions, logistical challenges and continuing protests, raising fresh concerns over the credibility of the electoral process.Polling was held across 21 constituencies, including nine in the Muzaffarabad Division of PoK and 12 refugee constituencies located in different parts of Pakistan.Voting was disrupted in several constituencies as road blockades and protests affected access to polling stations and delayed the electoral process.
Article Summary: Pakistani authorities have not officially confirmed the reported restrictions. The restrictions appear to target platforms covering the recent protests, alleged security crackdowns and growing public discontent in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) Earlier in July, a judicial magistrate's court in Islamabad ordered the blocking of several YouTube channels.

Article Title: 'Double tap': How terrorists are trapping Pakistan's security personnel
Article Text:
The latest assault came on Sunday, when a suicide bomber struck outside a police station in Swat's Kabal town during an anti-terror rally

A 'double tap' strategy to maximise casualties

Recent attacks expose worsening security crisis

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be the top priority to tackle rising security threats? Stronger intelligence and prevention Better emergency response 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan's security forces are increasingly facing a deadly challenge as militant groups adopt a "double tap" strategy that turns rescue missions into ambushes. The tactic, analysed by Pakistani newspaper Dawn, involves an initial attack on a police or security installation, followed by a second strike targeting reinforcements rushing to the scene.The evolving strategy has coincided with a sharp rise in militant violence, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where police and military personnel have repeatedly come under attack in recent months. The latest assault came on Sunday, when a suicide bomber struck outside a police station in Swat's Kabal town during an anti-terror rally, killing at least 14 people, including police personnel, and injuring 18 others.According to an analysis by Dawn, militants have refined their tactics by carrying out coordinated two-stage attacks aimed at inflicting the highest possible casualties on responding security forces.The first team attacks a police station, checkpost or security installation, drawing personnel into a firefight. Simultaneously, another militant group positions itself along likely reinforcement routes.As additional police or military teams rush to assist, they are targeted through improvised explosive devices (IEDs), roadside ambushes or quadcopters capable of dropping explosives.Dawn said predictable response patterns have repeatedly turned reinforcement teams into easy targets. Over the past three years, at least 16 police personnel, including three deputy superintendents of police (DSPs), have been killed while responding to attacks rather than during the initial assault.The newspaper pointed to the July 29 attack in Hangu district as the latest example. Terrorists first stormed a police checkpost before attacking the reinforcements sent to support officers already under fire. Nine police personnel, including DSP Diyar Khan, were killed and 28 others injured. According to Dawn, it was the third major incident in which the second phase of the attack caused the heaviest losses.The pattern dates back to January 2023, when DSP Sardar Hussain and two of his guards were killed in an IED blast while responding to an attack on the Sarband police station near Peshawar.The strategy has unfolded alongside a broader escalation in militant attacks across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.On July 24, at least 15 people, including 14 security personnel, were killed after Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) militants attacked a joint police checkpost in Tank district. According to Pakistan's military, the attackers first attempted to breach the facility but were repelled before ramming an explosives-laden vehicle into the perimeter wall, triggering a massive blast that destroyed much of the checkpost. Security forces said 15 militants were killed during the operation, while 12 soldiers, two policemen and a forest department official lost their lives.Sunday's suicide bombing in Swat further highlighted the deteriorating security environment. The attacker detonated explosives after police attempted to stop and search him outside the Kabal police station, according to Dawn. The blast occurred near a large public demonstration where residents had gathered to protest the resurgence of militancy and demand stronger state action.Speakers at the rally criticised authorities for failing to curb militant activity and urged the government to restore lasting peace in the valley, which was once cleared of insurgents after a major military operation but has seen renewed militant activity in recent months.Data cited by Dawn from the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies showed that Khyber Pakhtunkhwa recorded 154 terrorism-related deaths in July, more than double the 75 fatalities reported in June, underscoring the rapidly worsening security situation.
Article Summary: Pakistan's security forces are increasingly facing a deadly challenge. Militants adopt a 'double tap' strategy that turns rescue missions into ambushes. The tactic involves an initial attack on a police or security installation, followed by a second strike targeting reinforcements rushing to the scene.

Article Title: Peace rally in Pakistan rocked by suicide blast; 14 killed, 20 injured
Article Text:
The blast occurred near Kabal Chowk, where residents had assembled for the 'Olasi Pasoon' peace gathering

PTM condemns attack on peace gathering

Death toll rises as investigation begins

Attack shakes peace rally

Rising militant violence in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

Pakistani leaders condemn bombing

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is the main cause of the recent rise in militant violence in Swat? Political instability Lack of government action Economic disparity Influence of extremist groups 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

At least 14 people were killed and 20 others injured on Sunday when a suicide bomber struck outside the Kabal Police Station in Pakistan’s Swat district during a large public rally against terrorism, police officials said. The attacker detonated explosives after officers attempted to stop and search him at the entrance of the police station, triggering panic among hundreds of demonstrators gathered nearby.The blast occurred near Kabal Chowk, where residents had assembled for the “Olasi Pasoon” peace gathering to demand an end to the recent resurgence of militant violence in the Swat Valley.Soon after the bombing, PTM Momand said its social media team was launching a campaign condemning the attack on what it described as a peaceful gathering.“PTM socialMediaTeam is launching a campaign to condemn the horrific bomb blast that targeted Apeaceful gathering of ‘Olasi Pasoon’ in Swat. People who assembled to demand peace wr met with violence instead. Initial reports indicate at least seven pple killed #StopStateTerrorismInSwat,” the group posted on X.Swat police spokesperson Nasir Iqbal Karimi confirmed that 14 people had died in the explosion. Earlier, Swat Deputy Inspector General of Police Fida Hussain said seven people, including four police officers, had been killed and 20 injured, but the death toll was later revised upward.According to Swat District Police Officer Umar Khan, the bomber blew himself up after police personnel tried to search him at the station gate. He said security forces had cordoned off the area and launched an investigation to gather further evidence.The attack took place as the final speaker was addressing the gathering, causing widespread panic among those attending the rally. Rescue teams, police and local authorities rushed to the scene, and the injured were taken to Saidu Sharif Teaching Hospital for treatment. No group had claimed responsibility for the bombing by Sunday evening.Before the explosion, speakers at the rally had condemned the rise in militant activity and demanded that the government ensure lasting peace in the region. They said their movement had a single agenda, the restoration of peace and the elimination of terrorism from Swat.The speakers argued that maintaining law and order and eradicating terrorism were the responsibility of the state, and warned that continued insecurity could fuel broader public unrest. They also criticised the authorities for allegedly taking action against peaceful citizens while militants continued to operate in the mountainous areas of Swat.“Our children deserve education, and our families deserve to live in peace,” one speaker told the crowd.“We have witnessed years of bloodshed. Our mothers, sisters, and daughters have suffered immensely, and we do not want another generation of widows and orphans.”The bombing came amid a sharp increase in militant violence across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. Earlier on Sunday, an improvised explosive device blast near the Peshawar-Islamabad motorway toll plaza injured two police officers in Peshawar. On 30 July, nine police officers were killed in an attack on a police checkpost in Hangu.According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, excluding the merged districts, recorded 154 terrorism-related deaths in July, compared with 75 in June, an increase of 105 per cent.Pakistan President Asif Ali Zardari expressed sorrow over the loss of life and called for a comprehensive investigation into the bombing. He directed the relevant authorities to provide the best medical facilities to those injured.“Terrorists will never succeed in their nefarious efforts to harm peace, national unity, and the writ of the state,” he said, adding that the sacrifices of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police were a “source of pride for the entire nation”.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa governor Faisal Karim Kundi also condemned the attack, saying, “Terrorists cannot demoralise the nation with cowardly attacks.”Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's chief minister Sohail Afridi sought a report from the provincial Inspector General of Police and offered condolences to the families of the victims. “The elements hostile to peace will never be allowed to succeed in their nefarious intentions,” he said.
Article Summary: At least 14 people were killed and 20 others injured when a suicide bomber struck outside the Kabal Police Station in Pakistan’s Swat district. The attacker detonated explosives after officers attempted to stop and search him at the entrance of the police station. The blast occurred near Kabal Chowk, where residents had assembled for the ‘Olasi Pasoon’ peace gathering.

Article Title: 'Double standards': Pakistan rejects UN report on civilian casualties in Afghanistan strikes
Article Text:
Pakistan denies UN report that documents civilian casualties in Afghanistan, calls it 'baseless'

What the UN documented

Pakistan disputes UN findings

Pakistan's wider counterterrorism campaign

Pakistan’s military has rejected a UN report documenting hundreds of civilian casualties from cross-border fighting with Afghanistan, saying its forces targeted only Pakistani Taliban hideouts and other militant infrastructure and carried out the strikes in self-defence.Pakistan’s military spokesman Lt Gen Ahmad Sharif Chaudhry on Friday dismissed the findings as “baseless” and said Pakistani forces had not deliberately targeted civilians during operations against the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which Islamabad accuses of carrying out attacks from bases in Afghanistan.Chaudhry said Pakistan’s military had targeted “hideouts and infrastructure” used by the TTP and that those killed in the strikes were militants. He said the operations were necessary to protect people in Pakistan from attacks originating across the border.The comments came after the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) documented 499 civilians killed and 1,216 injured in cross-border armed violence between Afghanistan and Pakistan from October 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026.The UNAMA paper covering the latest quarter recorded 399 civilian casualties between April 1 and June 30 — 57 deaths and 342 injuries.Among them were 40 women and 112 children, including 26 children who were killed. UNAMA said the leading causes of civilian harm were airstrikes and ground engagements, and attributed all the cross-border civilian casualties it documented during the period to Pakistani security forces.The heaviest toll in the April-June period came from Pakistani airstrikes on June 28 in Paktya, Paktika and Kunar provinces, according to UNAMA. The strikes killed 28 civilians and injured 189 others, the report said.In one incident in Paktya's Chamkani district, UNAMA said a Pakistani airstrike hit a three-storey civilian residence. Residents gathered to rescue people trapped beneath the rubble, but a second airstrike struck the same location about 20 minutes later, while rescue efforts were under way.Chaudhry questioned the UN and Amnesty International reports, arguing that they relied heavily on accounts from Afghans despite what he described as restrictions on freedom of expression under Taliban rule.He also accused the Taliban government of allowing militant groups to operate from Afghan territory and said rights organisations had failed to adequately document attacks carried out against Pakistan.“These are double standards,” Chaudhry said, questioning how often rights groups had documented civilian casualties from US-led coalition airstrikes during the earlier war in Afghanistan.Chaudhry said Pakistan had recorded 3,145 terrorism incidents since January and that 2,084 militants had been killed, while 819 Pakistanis, including soldiers, police personnel and civilians, had died.He said Pakistani security forces had conducted 40,348 intelligence-based operations across the country during the same period.According to Chaudhry, Afghanistan-based militants had also carried out 28 suicide attacks in Pakistan since January. He alleged that many of those involved were Afghan nationals or people linked to Afghan security structures, and claimed some suicide bombers had been recruited from among drug users.Pakistan has vowed to continue its counterterrorism campaign, with Chaudhry saying the military would maintain operations against the TTP and affiliated groups.“We will continue these operations,” he said, adding that Pakistan was winning the fight against terrorism and would, “God willing”, win.
Article Summary: Pakistan’s military spokesman Lt Gen Ahmad Sharif Chaudhry dismissed the findings as ‘baseless’ He said Pakistani forces had not deliberately targeted civilians during operations against the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which Islamabad accuses of carrying out attacks from bases in Afghanistan.

Article Title: Rescuers find Nirmal Purja's body; all 10 climbers confirmed dead after avalanche on Broad Peak in PoK
Article Text:
Ten climbers, including Nirmal Purja, died in a Broad Peak avalanche. Search efforts continue for the remaining bodies after the incident.

Poll Vote & Share your view In your opinion, should documentaries about climbers and expeditions be more prevalent? Yes, they inspire others No, they glamorize risks 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja and nine other climbers swept away by an avalanche on PoK's Broad Peak have been confirmed dead, according to the Alpine Club of Pakistan and Purja's expedition company.Search and rescue teams are continuing efforts to recover the remaining bodies.The 10-member expedition was hit by an avalanche on Thursday while climbing Broad Peak in PoK's Gilgit-Baltistan region. Rescuers recovered three bodies on Friday after locating four, but harsh weather disrupted helicopter operations and delayed the search. Military-backed rescue teams resumed operations on Saturday."The world has lost one of mountaineering's greatest climbers," Purja's expedition company, Elite Exped, said in a statement. It added, "No words can ease the pain of this unimaginable loss."Confirming the tragedy, Alpine Club of Pakistan president Irfan Arshad Khan said, "The loss of these courageous climbers, who came from different nations united by their passion for the mountains, is an immeasurable loss to the global mountaineering fraternity."Paying tribute to rescuers, Khan said, "The mountains inspire us with their beauty, but they also remind us of the immense risks faced by those who venture into the high Himalaya and Karakoram."Earlier on Saturday, local police official Tahir Khan said the remains of Omani climber Nathira Ahmed were being flown to Islamabad, while the bodies of American climber Mallory Geis and Nepalese climber Bahadur Gurung remained at a hospital in Skardu.In a statement, Geis' family said, "Mallory was a bright light who was loved deeply by her family and friends. She will be profoundly missed."Purja, popularly known as Nims Dai, was a Nepal-born former British Army soldier who became one of the world's most celebrated mountaineers after scaling all 14 peaks above 8,000 metres in a record 189 days in 2019. The feat was documented in the Netflix film 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible. His record was surpassed in 2023.Describing Purja's legacy, Elite Exped said he was "a leader who inspired millions through his courage, humility and unwavering belief that human potential is far greater than we often imagine."The expedition marked Geis' first attempt at an 8,000-metre peak in PoK. It was also expected to be the final expedition for climber and guide Sakhi, who was also a geographer and high-altitude photographer, according to the Moving Mountains website.PoK's northern mountain ranges, including the Karakoram, are among the world's most challenging climbing destinations. Avalanches, falling ice and rocks, extreme altitude and rapidly changing weather frequently contribute to fatal accidents during expeditions.
Article Summary: The 10-member expedition was hit by an avalanche on Thursday while climbing Broad Peak in PoK's Gilgit-Baltistan region. Rescuers recovered three bodies on Friday after locating four, but harsh weather disrupted helicopter operations and delayed the search. Purja, popularly known as Nims Dai, was a Nepal-born former British Army soldier.

Article Title: Burnt-out vehicles, rock-strewn roads, heavy security: PoK votes in second phase amid unrest
Article Text:
The elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir (PoK) have been overshadowed by violence, allegations of electoral rigging and reports of enforced disappearances

Heavy security, protests overshadow polling

India rejects PoK polls

Poll Vote & Share your view Should India take a more active role in opposing the elections in PoK? Yes, definitely No, it's not necessary 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan conducted the second phase of legislative assembly elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) on Sunday amid fresh unrest, with residents reporting burnt vehicles, rock-strewn roads and heavy security across parts of Muzaffarabad following clashes between protesters and security forces.The voting is taking place in the second of three phases for the 45 directly elected seats of the 53-member assembly. However, the polls have been overshadowed by nearly two months of protests, allegations of election irregularities, political boycotts and a security crackdown.Residents of Muzaffarabad said fresh violence ahead of polling had raised concerns that the unrest would dominate the election process. Local reports described burnt-out vehicles, roads blocked with rocks and a strong presence of police, paramilitary personnel and army troops in several areas after clashes between demonstrators and security forces.Pakistan has deployed a three-tier security arrangement across PoK, with police, Pakistan Rangers, the Federal Constabulary and around 2,100 army personnel guarding polling stations.The elections come against the backdrop of sustained protests led by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), which has been demanding greater political freedoms, economic reforms and the abolition of 12 assembly seats reserved for Pakistan-based refugees.The group has also sought better healthcare, education, employment opportunities and reduced political privileges.JAAC has boycotted the elections, arguing that the reserved refugee seats allow Pakistan's mainstream political parties to influence government formation in the region.The protest movement has intensified in recent weeks after talks with the authorities collapsed, leading to large demonstrations, strikes and clashes. Polling in two constituencies was postponed because of the deteriorating security situation.Rights groups, including the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, the United Nations and Amnesty International, have criticised the crackdown on protesters, internet restrictions and the ban imposed on JAAC under anti-terrorism laws.India has rejected the elections, describing them as a 'cosmetic' exercise aimed at legitimising Pakistan's 'illegal occupation' of the region.External affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the entire Union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, including areas under Pakistan's control are an integral part of India.He said the elections were an attempt by Pakistan to 'camouflage its illegal occupation' and conceal alleged human rights violations in the region."The current cosmetic electoral exercise is nothing but an attempt by Pakistan to camouflage its illegal occupation and hide its grave human rights violations in the region. The ongoing mass protest in the Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir is the direct consequence of its economic exploitation, its denial of fundamental rights to the people and its administrative oppression," Jaiswal had said earlier this week.
Article Summary: Pakistan conducted the second phase of legislative assembly elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) on Sunday. Residents reported burnt vehicles, rock-strewn roads and heavy security across parts of Muzaffarabad. The voting is taking place in the second of three phases for the 45 directly elected seats of the 53-member assembly. The polls have been overshadowed by nearly two months of protests, allegations of election irregularities, political boycotts and a security crackdown.

Article Title: ‘Cockroaches’ and crackdowns: Can Pakistan’s Gen Z storm the barricades?
Article Text:
Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Asim Munir

The warning from within

A year-wise snapshot of terror attacks in Pakistan, with 2025 recording the highest number in more than a decade.

The uniform behind the curtain

A country of fragmented rebellions

A terrorised society

The Global Terrorism Index 2026 ranks Pakistan as the country most affected by terrorism among 163 nations.

Where is Imran Khan now?

Beaten into submission

What’s next

Poll Vote & Share your view Would you support a unified movement from Gen Z in Pakistan? Absolutely Probably not 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Just look at what is happening in Pakistan -occupied Kashmir. People have taken to the streets over bread-and-butter issues and local election grievances. At least 40 protesters have died this week alone. To add insult to injury, Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif has described these protesters as “enemies” like India and ruled out dialogue with them."Its absolute disdain for the innocent people of PoK was laid bare when the defence minister branded the protesting civilians as enemies," external affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said. He said the “so-called” elections represented a “humiliating rejection” of the Pakistani establishment. "We urge that the international community should scrutinise Pakistan's actions and hold it accountable for its atrocities," Jaiswal added.And yet, the violence has barely registered internationally. Some foreign media outlets have offered customary coverage, often with the expected tilt, but it has largely been treated as business as usual in Pakistan. No professional outrage merchants or loud global campaigners have mounted a sustained protest against the conduct of the Pakistani army.Expectations from Pakistan are now so low that even the use of lethal force against its own people struggles to move the global news cycle.That silence says plenty about how the world views Pakistan. But the more interesting question is how Pakistanis see these protests themselves.Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi may have inadvertently supplied part of the answer.“Whether you agree or not, the system we have been living under has collapsed,” Naqvi said at event.But his most revealing remark came when he talked about Gen Z. “If these ‘Cockroaches’ get united, they can turn everything upside down,” Naqvi said.With around 60% of its population under 30 and an estimated 65-70 million people belonging to Gen Z, Pakistan appears, on paper, primed for a youth revolt. So why hasn’t Pakistan produced a nationwide Gen Z movement?Pakistan is a “hybrid regime”, as its own commentators describe it. Over the past two years, the army has moved beyond being informally supreme and begun formalising its dominance. A constitutional amendment created the post of chief of defence forces for the army chief, placing the navy and air force under him as well. His tenure was extended, and he was elevated to field marshal with what amounts to lifetime immunity from prosecution.None of this required a coup. It was delivered through a compliant civilian coalition of the PML-N and PPP that increasingly resembles the administrative wing of military rule rather than an elected government.The real genius of the military’s political arrangement has been its creation of an endless game of musical chairs. When one civilian face becomes unpopular, the establishment replaces it with another: the PPP, the Sharifs, Imran Khan , and then back again.This constant rotation serves a specific purpose. It prevents public anger from consolidating into a single grievance against the military establishment. Responsibility is repeatedly shifted to the civilian face of the day. When things go wrong, the answer offered is not structural change but another saviour, another party and another election promising to fix everything.For Gen Z, therefore, there is no clean and accessible target around which a national protest movement can form. A young Pakistani can be angry with a leader or political party. But the military, the country’s true centre of power, remains officially apolitical and practically beyond reach.Pakistan does not lack dissent. Its dissent is fragmented by geography, ideology and competing objectives.In Balochistan, the Baloch Liberation Army and its supporters are waging a separatist insurgency. The Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan is not fighting for democratic accountability; it seeks the imposition of Sharia law and the overthrow of the constitutional order. A Baloch nationalist, a TTP sympathiser and a university student in Lahore or Karachi protesting unemployment are unlikely to assemble beneath one banner or chant the same slogans.The state, therefore, does not need to defeat one unified movement. It only needs to prevent several incompatible movements from recognising that they are confronting the same power structure.That fragmentation also allows the establishment to treat every form of dissent differently: terrorism in one province, separatism in another, political disorder elsewhere and foreign conspiracy almost everywhere.Then there is the grim reality that Pakistan has become one of the world’s most terror-ravaged countries. The Global Terrorism Index 2026 ranked it as the country most affected by terrorism. Pakistan recorded over 1,000 terror-related deaths in 2025, its worst figures since 2013.This security crisis gives the army both political legitimacy and operational cover. Terrorism becomes the justification for an expanded military role, while dissent can be blurred with insurgency or branded “anti-state”. Extraordinary force is presented as an unavoidable response to extraordinary danger.The repression is often brutal but bureaucratically administered: Sedition cases, enforced disappearances, media blackouts, internet restrictions and the permanent threat of being labelled a traitor.Pakistan’s Gen Z has already seen what happens when a genuinely popular political leader crosses the establishment.For many young and urban Pakistanis, Imran Khan became a vehicle for expressing anger against a closed political system. His removal from power and the crackdown that followed offered a textbook lesson in the cost of direct confrontation.Look at where Khan is now. The hybrid regime is actively trying to neutralise the country’s most internationally recognisable political figure. If the establishment can do that to Imran Khan, what chance does an ordinary young Pakistani believe he has?If it comes to its survival, the regime would not mind killing even thousands.Reports of enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings of Baloch and Pashtun activists surface with alarming regularity. Students, political workers, journalists and human rights defenders are reported missing after alleged abductions. Some are later found dead, their bodies bearing signs of torture.Pakistan’s own commission of inquiry documented more than 10,000 cases of enforced disappearance between 2011 and early 2024.For young Baloch and Pashtuns, the message could hardly be clearer: Challenging the state may result not merely in arrest, but in disappearance.This explains why Pakistan may not witness a Gen Z uprising in the classic sense: Millions occupying the streets, facing down the state and forcing a negotiated reset.Naqvi is right about one thing: if Pakistan’s young people unite, they could turn the system upside down. That is precisely why the system has spent decades ensuring they remain divided, disillusioned and afraid.Elsewhere, Gen Z has taken to the streets to reclaim its future from misrule. In Pakistan, it is being taught that survival itself may be the most it can hope for.
Article Summary: Pakistan is a ‘hybrid regime’, as its own commentators describe it. With around 60% of its population under 30 and an estimated 65-70 million people belonging to Gen Z, Pakistan appears, on paper, primed for a youth revolt. So why hasn't Pakistan produced a nationwide Gen Z movement?

Article Title: ‘Dhurandhar’ gangster’s brother shot in Karachi
Article Text:
Personal enmity or gang war? Probe on into hit on Zubair Baloch

Zubair Baloch — the brother of jailed Pakistan gangster Uzair Baloch, whose ruthless ascent was dramatised in the movie ‘Dhurandhar’ — is learned to be critically wounded following a targeted drive-by shooting in Karachi’s Lyari neighbourhood on Thursday evening, reports .The 40-year-old was sitting outside his Singu Lane home when two masked assailants on a motorcycle opened fire, striking him in the chest and abdomen.Zubair was rushed to Civil Hospital Karachi for emergency surgery. Two bystanders were also injured in the crossfire, with one reported to be in serious condition.According to Pakistan police, the attackers fled after a nearby shopkeeper returned fire. CCTV footage from the spot, which surfaced on Telegram channels, showed chaos on the street as the gunmen escaped.Police told the local press they were probing angles of personal enmity and the potential resurgence of long-standing gang wars.Zubair, arrested in multiple criminal cases in 2012, was released from prison last year, while his brother Uzair remains in jail serving a 12-year sentence handed down by a military court.Uzair and several accomplices were indicted for a 2012 armed attack on law enforcement officers under Kalakot police station’s jurisdiction.In April 2020, Uzair Baloch received a 12-year prison sentence for espionage.For decades, the historic Karachi neighbourhood of Lyari served as the epicentre of a gang war and a hub of organised crime. The turmoil traces back to early turf battles over drug trade routes and extortion rackets, which eventually expanded into a high-stakes proxy war involving major political factions.Notorious figures such as Sardar Abdul Rehman Baloch aka Rehman Dakait and his fierce rival Arshad Pappu turned narrow alleyways into battlegrounds, leveraging strategic political patronage through outfits like Peoples’ Aman Committee to insulate their syndicates from police oversight. Following Rehman Dakait’s death in a 2009 police encounter, his cousin Uzair Baloch stepped in to control the dominant faction.
Article Summary: Zubair Baloch, 40, was shot in the chest and abdomen on Thursday evening. He was sitting outside his home when two masked assailants opened fire. Two bystanders were also injured in the crossfire, with one reported to be in serious condition. Police are probing angles of personal enmity and the potential resurgence of gang wars.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Chandrika Kumaratunga: 'Power is a joke, but it gives me the authority to do what I think I need to do for the country'
Article Text:
Quote of the day by former Sri Lankan president Chandrika Kumaratunga.

Daughter of two PMs who claimed to have disliked power

Chandrika Kumaratunga 's political journey

When Chandrika Bandaranaike Kumaratunga sat down with Australian journalist Michael Maher in July 2005 for an interview on the ABC program Foreign Correspondent, her presidency was drawing to a close. Asked about the allure of supreme political office, Sri Lanka’s first female president brushed aside the notion that she was captivated by high status. It's always mesmerizing to study how powerful people of the world perceive power. And Kumaratunga said: "I'm a workaholic, I like to work. And I'm in this, not to fill my pockets like lots of others, or because the idea of power thrills me - I find it a joke.""Yes. I find power a joke - I laugh or I get very angry with it," she doubled down.Michael Maher was surprised and called the president a rare politician who does not like power and called it a joke. "I don't like it at all. The only thing that attracts me in power is that it gives me the authority and the possibility of doing what I think should be done for this country," Kumaratunga said.To evaluate this statement, one must look at the extraordinary personal tragedy and political inheritance that shaped her worldview.Born into Sri Lanka’s ultimate political dynasty, she was the daughter of two prime ministers: Solomon West Ridgeway Dias Bandaranaike, who was assassinated by a Buddhist monk in 1959, and Sirimavo Bandaranaike, the world’s first female prime minister.Political power was not an abstract concept or a distant goal for her; it was the atmosphere of her childhood home. Yet it was also the primary source of immense personal loss. Her life was repeatedly upended by political violence. After her father’s assassination, she studied in Paris, absorbing political science and left-leaning intellectual traditions away from the intense glare of Colombo politics.Upon returning to Sri Lanka, she allied herself with Vijaya Kumaratunga, a charismatic actor-turned-radical politician who broke away from the traditional establishment to champion ethnic reconciliation. In 1988, Vijaya, also Chandrika's husband, was brutally assassinated on their doorstep by political extremists.Eleven years later, while serving as president, Chandrika herself was targeted by a suicide bomber from the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam during an election rally, surviving the blast but losing vision in her right eye.When someone whose father and husband were both murdered by political violence says that power is a joke, the sentiment carries a distinct, cynical weight.From her perspective, political authority was an absurd, dangerous theater that brought immense personal suffering rather than genuine fulfillment. It was an instrument to be endured rather than celebrated, useful only for the structural authority it granted to implement policy. Yet this insistence on being a reluctant steward of power stands in sharp tension with the political reality of her governance.In the same 2005 television feature, her sister, Sunethra Bandaranaike, offered a starkly different portrait, suggesting that despite her claims of disliking authority, Chandrika loved power, thrived on it, and treated it like an addictive drug. This internal family dynamic captured the dual identity that defined her presidency.Sweeping into office in 1994 on a massive public mandate, Chandrika promised to end the long-running civil war through negotiation and to roll back the authoritarian executive presidential system established by the United National Party. She framed her ascension as a mission to re-humanize Sri Lankan politics and resolve the ethnic conflict through devolution. However, when early peace talks with the Tamil Tigers collapsed in 1995, her administration pivoted to an aggressive policy known as "war for peace," launching heavy military offensives in the north while attempting to push through constitutional reforms.Throughout her eleven years in power, she proved to be a shrewd and uncompromising politician. Far from treating the executive presidency as a lightweight burden, she utilized its vast constitutional powers to navigate bitter parliamentary feuds, manipulate party coalitions, and manage complex military campaigns.In 2003, when her political rival Ranil Wickremesinghe served as prime minister during a fragile ceasefire, she invoked her executive prerogatives to seize control of key ministries, demonstrating a fierce grasp on state authority when she felt her vision for the nation was threatened.Her statement to Michael Maher encapsulates the fundamental paradox of her legacy. On one level, viewing power as a joke reflected the philosophical detachment of someone who had seen the lethal consequences of political ambition firsthand. On another level, claiming that power only mattered as a tool to execute her personal vision for the country highlighted the executive paternalism that often defined her reign. It reflected a deep conviction that she alone understood what Sri Lanka required, transforming political authority from a personal desire into an absolute necessity.
Article Summary: Chandrika Bandaranaike Kumaratunga was Sri Lanka's first female president. Her father and husband were both murdered by political violence. She was targeted by a suicide bomber during an election rally. She served as prime minister during a fragile ceasefire in 2003.

Article Title: Bangladesh seeks India’s stand on Sheikh Hasina’s Aug 5 virtual address
Article Text:
Former Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina (AP image)

DHAKA: Ahead of former Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina ’s likely Aug 5 virtual address, state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam Monday asked India to clarify whether it supports the online meeting of the Awami League chief.The event at Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia in Delhi will be Hasina’s first public appearance, exactly two years after massive protests led to her govt’s ouster and she fled Bangladesh.“We are moving forward with India with a forward-looking approach. We don’t want it to be damaged, and I firmly believe that India doesn’t want it either. So, India has to clarify whether it is supporting it or not,” she said while addressing reporters at ministry of foreign affairs.Asked about Hasina and other Awami League members staying abroad, the minister stressed though Indian govt is not organising the programme, “India has to clarify because they are in India.”Meanwhile, PM Tarique Rahman’s foreign affairs adviser Humaiun Kobir, during a meeting with Indian high commissioner Dinesh Trivedi at Prime Minister’s Office Monday, said Dhaka expects New Delhi’s cooperation in ensuring that any person from the banned Awami League, including Hasina, does not use Indian territory to make political statements or conduct activities aimed at creating instability within Bangladesh.Shama Obaed said Bangladesh could “communicate” with India on the event if it considers it necessary. “Dhaka does not want the issue to undermine bilateral relations,” she said, claiming New Delhi had indicated it did not expect a fugitive accused to make political statements from Indian territory — Hasina has been sentenced to death.She said political activities by fugitives from India that seek to create instability in Bangladesh could negatively affect bilateral relations. Asked about the invitation to PM Tarique Rahman to attend Brics Summit in Sept in Delhi, she indicated no decision had been taken yet.
Article Summary: The event at Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia in Delhi will be Hasina’s first public appearance. It will be exactly two years after massive protests led to her govt's ouster and she fled Bangladesh. Bangladesh could “communicate” with India on the event if it considers it necessary.

Article Title: Watch: Broad Peak avalanche that killed record-breaking mountaineer Nirmal Purja and his crew
Article Text:
Footage captures the moment a catastrophic avalanche swept down Broad Peak on 30th July, resulting in 10 fatalities. (Source: @karakoramvision)

What happened on Broad Peak?

Who was Nirmal Purja ?

Pakistan-based tour operator Karakoram Vision said the visuals were captured from base camp on July 30 as the group climbed the mountain. It claimed an avalanche struck above the climbers and that no one was visible after the snow cleared. The visuals have not been independently authenticated.The avalanche at about 5,700 metres swept away the 10-member expedition on Thursday on Broad Peak, an 8,051-metre mountain in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir’s Gilgit-Baltistan region and the world’s 12th-highest peak.The group included climbers from Nepal, Pakistan, the US, Oman and China.Ground and military-backed rescue teams searched the mountain with helicopters and drones, but poor weather and hazardous terrain hampered operations. By Sunday, rescuers had located eight bodies, including Purja’s, while teams continued searching for the remaining two climbers and worked to bring the bodies down.Purja, 43, was a Nepal-born British mountaineer and former British Army soldier. He climbed the world’s 14 highest peaks in a record 189 days in 2019, an achievement featured in the Netflix documentary 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible. The record was broken in 2023.He was also part of the all-Nepali team that completed the first winter ascent of K2 in 2021.Prince William was among those who paid tribute, describing Purja as one of the world’s greatest mountaineers and offering condolences to the families of those killed.
Article Summary: Nirmal Purja, 43, was a Nepal-born British mountaineer and former British Army soldier. He climbed the world’s 14 highest peaks in a record 189 days in 2019, an achievement featured in the Netflix documentary 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible.

Article Title: Hasina may make her first public appearance this week since ouster
Article Text:
Former Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina (AP image)

Exactly two years after her ouster from office, former Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina may make her first public appearance this week. Hasina is likely to virtually address an event at the foreign correspondents’ club of South Asia in New Delhi on Aug 5.Hasina fled to India from Bangladesh on the same day two years ago, after clashes between protesters and pro-govt groups along with a security crackdown resulted in hundreds of deaths, leading to widespread public outrage. However, Hasina announced recently that she would be returning to Bangladesh later this year. Dhaka continues to raise diplomatically the issue of her extradition with India.While Hasina has been giving written interviews from Delhi, this would be her first public address since she landed in India. While New Delhi maintains that Hasina is not allowed to carry out political activities from India, Dhaka believes her statements against the BNP govt before the media can stymie efforts by both sides for a pragmatic reset in the relationship.
Article Summary: Sheikh Hasina is likely to virtually address an event at the foreign correspondents’ club of South Asia in New Delhi on Aug 5. Hasina fled to India from Bangladesh on the same day two years ago, after clashes between protesters and pro-govt groups.

Article Title: Sheikh Hasina ouster anniversary: Bangladesh issues nationwide alert over attack on police
Article Text:
Security personnel stand guard outside a police station in Dhaka as Bangladesh steps up security amid alerts of possible attacks on law enforcement vehicles. (Reuters photo)

Bangladesh Police has issued a nationwide alert warning of possible terrorist or extremist attacks targeting law enforcement vehicles, citing intelligence inputs ahead of the second anniversary of the ouster of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina's government.The Operations Control Branch (OCB) issued the internal directive on Saturday, instructing police units across the country to tighten security for official vehicles. The directive did not specify the source of the threat.A Bangladesh Police Headquarters (PHQ) official said security measures had been intensified nationwide."In line with a directive of our OCB, police units enforced the tightened vigil throughout Bangladesh against possible sabotage targeting particularly police vehicles, including jeeps, trucks and buses," the official said.The directive instructed officers to ensure the security of official vehicles while they were in motion and when parked. It also said vehicles stopped temporarily must be kept in secure locations under constant supervision."No government vehicle should be left unattended...even inside police stations," the official said, citing the directive.The alert comes days before August 5, which marks the second anniversary of the violent student-led protests that toppled Sheikh Hasina's Awami League government in 2024 and forced her to flee to India.Despite the heightened alert, Counter Terrorism and Transnational Crime unit chief Mohammad Shamsul Haque said his agency had not received any specific intelligence about sabotage plans linked to the anniversary.He said the unit remained on maximum alert.The security advisory follows a series of recent bomb scares in Dhaka. Police recently defused a remote-controlled explosive device concealed inside an abandoned umbrella at the Motijheel metro station, while two unattended bags found at separate metro stations were later found to contain only betel leaves and tobacco.After Hasina's removal from power, Bangladesh's interim government barred the Awami League from contesting elections through an executive order.Speaking at a police event in Rajshahi on Sunday, Bangladesh home minister Salahuddin Ahmed said authorities were thoroughly investigating every incident involving suspicious objects."The overall law and order situation remained under control and that the government was maintaining the highest level of vigilance despite a decline in sabotage-related incidents," he said.His remarks came a day after global crowd-sourced database Numbeo ranked Dhaka as the most unsafe and crime-prone major city in South Asia in its Mid-2026 Crime Index.
Article Summary: Bangladesh Police issues alert warning of possible terrorist or extremist attacks on law enforcement vehicles. The alert comes days before August 5, which marks the second anniversary of the violent student-led protests that toppled Sheikh Hasina's Awami League government.

Article Title: Nirmal Purja — star climber, elite British officer & MBE — dead on PoK peak
Article Text:
Purja, who died five days after his 43rd birthday, had been attempting to become the first mountaineer to climb all 14 eight-thousanders twice without supplemental oxygen

Nepal-born British mountaineer Nirmal ‘Nimsdai’ Purja, 43, died with nine other climbers after an avalanche struck the 8,047m Broad Peak in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) on July 30, only nine days after he became the first person to scale Gasherbrum II (8,035 metres) without supplemental oxygen. Elite Exped, the agency Purja co-founded, confirmed Saturday afternoon that all 10 members of the international team had died and there were no survivors, though authorities had not recovered all the bodies. Victims of the Karakoram tragedy included six Nepalese and one climber each from Pakistan, Oman, US and China.Purja, who died five days after his 43rd birthday, had been attempting to become the first mountaineer to climb all 14 eight-thousanders twice without supplemental oxygen. The ascent of Gasherbrum II on July 21 marked his 57th ascent of an 8,000m peak and his 29th without bottled oxygen. He then made a last-minute decision to attempt nearby Broad Peak during the same PoK expedition.Born in Myagdi district in 1983 and raised in Chitwan — in Nepal’s plains — Purja later became a British citizen. He spent 16 years in the British military, serving with Brigade of Gurkhas before becoming the first Gurkha to join Special Boat Service, Royal Navy’s special forces unit.Queen Elizabeth II appointed him MBE in 2018.Purja began his climbing journey in 2012 with what was meant to be a trek to Everest Base Camp but pushed beyond the original plan and turned the hike into a summit attempt. The experience became an early lesson in ambition and endurance. He first summited Mount Everest in 2016 and returned to the summit five more times, the last ascent occurring earlier this year.The climber, mourned by mountaineers across the world, entered history books in 2019 by climbing all 14 peaks above 8,000m in six months and six days, smashing a record that had stood at nearly eight years. His extraordinary life was immortalised by the Netflix documentary ‘14 Peaks’. Purja would later complete all 14 without supplemental oxygen and joined the all-Nepalese team that made K2’s first winter ascent in Jan 2021.In a Facebook post days before his death, Purja wrote, “This was never the plan. Initially, the plan was to climb just G2,” adding that a successful Broad Peak ascent would leave only Cho Oyu in his record bid. He ended the post with a line that became poignant after the disaster: “Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down. I take zero mountains for granted. Not one.”Purja had launched ‘Hat-Trick Project’ last year with the extraordinary aim of climbing all 14 eight-thousanders and Seven Summits three times each.The other Nepalese victims included Pur Bahadur Gurung, known as Yukta; Kili Pemba Sherpa, Nima Sherpa, Nawang Thindu Sherpa and Gyalu Sherpa. Omani climber Nadhira Ahmed Al Harthy, American Mallory Geis, Pakistani climber Sohail Sakhi and China’s Wang Zhong also died. Al Harthy was the first Omani woman to scale Everest, while Geis was attempting her first 8,000m peak in PoK. Sakhi, a geographer, guide and high-altitude photographer, was undertaking what was expected to be his final expedition.Purja and his team’s geo trackers showed climbers losing hundreds of metres in altitude before their signals stopped around 9am on Thursday. His tracker later appeared to change location, briefly raising hopes that he might have survived. Search teams used drones to locate bodies as bad weather and avalanche danger hampered operations.Paying tribute, Nepal PM Balendra Shah said, “The Himalayas grant the glory of the peak to many, and sometimes hold them forever in their embrace,” adding that Purja and the other climbers would remain immortal through their bravery and contribution.Reinhold Messner, the legendary Italian alpinist widely regarded as one of the greatest high-altitude climbers in history, also paid tribute to Purja. Now 81, Messner, who was the first person to summit all 14 eight-thousanders without supplementary oxygen and helped establish the minimalist alpine style in the Himalayas, said, “Nims chose his own path with courage and passion. What remains is not only the sorrow of his passing, but the memory of a life truly lived. My thoughts are with his family, his friends, and everyone who had the privilege of knowing him.”------------------Nimsdai’s Record Trail-----------------------Summited all 14 8-thousanders in 189 days in 2019All 8-thousanders without supplemental oxygen in 2 years, 5 months in 2024First to summit K2 in winter in Jan 2021Everest, Lhotse, Makalu in 2 days, 30 minutes57 successful 8-thousander ascents29 8-thousander ascents without supplemental oxygenFirst Gurkha to serve with UK’s Special Boat ServiceMBE for services to high-altitude mountaineering in 2018
Article Summary: Nirmal ‘Nimsdai’ Purja, 43, died with nine other climbers after an avalanche struck the 8,047m Broad Peak in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. Victims of the Karakoram tragedy included six Nepalese and one climber each from Pakistan, Oman, US and China. He had been attempting to become the first mountaineer to climb all 14 eight-thousanders twice without supplemental oxygen.

Article Title: Mountaineer Nirmal Purja killed in avalanche on PoK peak, says his company
Article Text:
Nepalese mountaineering icon Nirmal Purja (file photo) has been confirmed dead after an avalanche on Broad Peak

Nirmal “Nims Dai” Purja, the legendary Nepal-born mountaineer who climbed all 14 of the world’s 8,000-metre peaks in a record six months and six days, has been confirmed dead after an avalanche struck his expedition on PoK’s Broad Peak.Purja, 43, was confirmed dead on Saturday by his expedition company Elite Exped, ending a two-day search operation after the avalanche swept a group of climbers down the 8,047-metre mountain on Thursday.“It is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal ‘Nimsdai’ Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak,” Elite Exped said in a statement.The company also confirmed the deaths of Purja’s climbing partners and guides, Pur Bahadur Gurung, known as “Yukta”, and Nima Sherpa. Other members of the expedition were also killed in the avalanche.Nepal PM Balendra Shah paid tribute to Purja and his fellow climbers climbers killed on Broad Peak. In a post, Shah said mountaineering was not merely about reaching a summit but represented “courage, discipline, sacrifice and the indomitable confidence to challenge human limits”. He said the climbers’ courage and dedication would remain an enduring source of inspiration.He offered his condolences to the deceased climbers and expressed sympathy to their families, relatives and well-wishers.The avalanche struck on July 30 as the expedition climbed between Camp 2 and higher elevations on Broad Peak in PoK’s Karakoram range. The entire team lost communication after the avalanche, while rescue efforts were hampered by poor weather and the danger of further avalanches.Tracking data showed Purja at about 6,660 metres shortly before the avalanche. His device later indicated a sharp drop in altitude, suggesting he had been swept hundreds of metres down the mountain. The signal subsequently stopped.Military helicopters and ground teams led by experienced Nepali climbers joined the search. Rescuers located several of the missing climbers, but none showed signs of life. Recovery teams continued searching for the remaining missing climbers.Purja had been attempting to add Broad Peak to an already extraordinary climbing record. In 2019, he completed all 14 of the world's peaks above 8,000 metres in six months and six days as part of his Project Possible expedition, breaking the previous record of more than seven years.He later became the fastest climber to complete all 14 eight-thousanders without supplementary oxygen and was attempting to become the first person to climb all 14 twice without supplemental oxygen.A former British Gurkha and Special Boat Service soldier, Purja entered mountaineering after a 2012 trek to Everest Base Camp. His 2019 record-breaking expedition was later chronicled in the Netflix documentary “14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible”, bringing him international recognition.Purja was also part of the Nepali team that made the first winter ascent of K2 in January 2021. He later founded Elite Exped and the Nimsdai Foundation and became a prominent advocate for Nepali climbers and high-altitude workers.His death came days after he wrote on Instagram that he was seeking “nothing but safe passage” up and down Broad Peak, adding that he took no mountain for granted. His passing is a great loss to the mountaineering community and the people of Nepal.
Article Summary: Nepalese mountaineer Nirmal Purja has been confirmed dead after an avalanche on Broad Peak. The 43-year-old climbed all 14 of the world’s 8,000-metre peaks in a record six months and six days. Other members of the expedition were also killed in the avalanche.
